analysis:
The largest failure category is false_positive_earlier, with 11 of 15 failures. Retrieval is fine (recall@k 0.95) and the verifier almost never misses the true quote (verifier recall 0.98). The problem is that it also accepts an earlier candidate that only partly overlaps with the claim. There are three recurring patterns:
(a) The same speaker makes a related but different statement. The candidate shares one element with the claim but is missing the claim's distinctive elements, or swaps them for other ones.
(b) An unattributed ("None") candidate makes a generic remark on the same theme but with different specifics. The current prompt says "judge mainly by content", which in practice gives these a free pass.
(c) A commentary or tweet that describes the speaker's view, rather than the speaker's own quoted words.
Some cases are arguably label noise: an earlier, longer version of the same quotation is really the same statement. I don't think we should try to fix those.

The fix is a stricter verifier prompt. A candidate should match only if it contains all of the claim's distinctive elements; sharing one element or a theme is not enough. Unattributed candidates should need content that clearly matches, not just fits. Earlier or longer versions of the same quotation should still count, so we don't lose real matches. This doesn't change the number of verifier calls.

The not_retrieved failures (3) are heavy paraphrases with almost no word overlap, which BM25 can't fix cheaply. Increasing k together with the speaker filter was already tried and rejected.

rationale: Targets false_positive_earlier (11 of 15 failures). The rule changes from 'central fact, judge mainly by content' to 'all of the claim's distinctive elements must be present'. It explicitly rules out candidates that share only one element or the theme, stricter checks on unattributed candidates, and third-party descriptions. It keeps matches for longer or earlier versions of the same quotation, which protects verifier recall. Verifier calls stay the same.

changes.value:
You check whether quotations from news coverage are the source of a claim.

The claim reports something a speaker said. Each candidate is a quotation with its attributed speaker and the date it was first seen. Decide for each candidate whether the claim could be a report of THAT quotation.

First, identify the claim's distinctive elements: the specific assertion plus any particular details it mentions (events, actions, named things, figures, time references, conditions, contrasts). Then a candidate MATCHES only if:
- it contains ALL of those distinctive elements (the claim may paraphrase, reword or summarise, and may cover only part of a longer quotation), and
- it makes the same point, with no conflicting or substituted details.

A longer, shorter or slightly differently transcribed version of the same quotation counts as a match.

A candidate does NOT match if:
- it shares only one element, a theme or some vocabulary with the claim, but lacks the claim's other specific details;
- it is a related but different statement by the same speaker (e.g. a different step, argument or occasion);
- it is a generic remark consistent with the claim but not specifically stating it;
- it is someone else's description or commentary about the speaker's view, rather than the speaker's own words;
- it concerns a different event, period or figure, or makes a different or opposite point.

Speaker attributions are automatic and sometimes wrong or missing ("None"). A clearly different speaker does NOT match. For a "None" candidate, require that its content clearly matches the claim's specific wording or details, not just fits with it.

When in doubt, do not match. Return the ids of all matching candidates (an empty list if none).

rationale: A lighter version of the same fix, in case the full rewrite costs too much recall. It keeps the current prompt structure and only adds three things: the all-distinctive-details requirement, the 'related but different statement by the same speaker' exclusion, and a stricter rule for 'None' speakers and third-party commentary. Targets false_positive_earlier. Verifier calls stay the same.

changes.value:
You check whether quotations from news coverage state the same fact as a claim.

Each candidate is a quotation with its attributed speaker and the date it was first seen. A candidate MATCHES if the speaker, in that quotation, asserts the claim's statement: same event, action, figure or position, and it contains every specific detail the claim reports, with no conflicting key details. The claim may paraphrase or summarise the quotation, or cover only part of it; a longer or slightly different version of the same quotation still matches.

Speaker attributions are automatic and sometimes wrong or missing ("None"). A clearly different speaker making a similar statement does NOT match. An unattributed candidate matches only if its content is clearly the same statement, not merely compatible with it. A third party describing or commenting on the speaker's view does NOT match.

A candidate does NOT match if it is only on the same topic, shares some but not all of the claim's specific details, is a related but different statement by the same speaker, makes a different or opposite point, concerns a different event, period or figure, or is a generic remark the claim does not report.

Return the ids of all matching candidates (an empty list if none).

analysis:
The largest category is false_positive_earlier (14 of 17 failures). The verifier finds every true quote (verifier_recall 1.0), but it also accepts earlier candidates. Most of those wrong matches are near-verbatim variants from the same speaker: the Bergeron, Saif Ali Khan and Sekulow cases are the same remark worded differently, or a fuller or truncated version of it. The rest are close paraphrases from the same speaker about the same event, such as Schiff's "apply the facts to the law" or Netanyahu's "fighting the coronavirus war". I can't fix these well with retrieval knobs. The candidates come from the right speaker and rank high in BM25, so changing k or adding a speaker filter won't remove them. A real fix needs a stricter verifier prompt, which this line can't change. Some of these cases may also be gold-label problems, where the 'true' first appearance is really a later re-report of a remark that was already in coverage.

Given that, the best I can do with the retrieval knobs is make small gains and cut verifier calls. Each knob has failed on its own (speaker_filter=surname: net +2; k=20: net +1; k=15: recall dropped). Combining them is a materially new change. The surname filter drops candidates from clearly different speakers, which removes some false positives that don't come from the same speaker. If the filter is applied before the top-k cut, the cut slots go to quotes from the right speaker, which should limit the recall loss from a smaller k and lower calls per claim.

The 3 not_retrieved failures are paraphrase cases where the claim's wording differs from the quote ("hopeful" for "optimistic", "grave matter" for "serious problem"). Here BM25 mostly matches on the speaker's name, so the true quote can sit just below the cutoff. A larger k with the surname filter could recover them. The k=50+surname test was done under the old query template and index, so the result may differ under the current setup.

With the filter on, the top 20 are mostly from the right speaker, which should limit the recall loss seen at k=15. Fewer near-duplicate distractors are shown to the verifier, and calls per claim should drop.

analysis:
There are 14 false_positive_earlier failures and 3 not_retrieved, so false_positive_earlier is the biggest category. These knobs can't fix it, though. In every false_positive_earlier example shown, the wrong match comes from the same speaker as the true quote, and in most cases it is an earlier, longer or reworded version of the same statement (Bergeron, Saif Ali Khan, Sekulow, Netanyahu). In others it is a closely related remark from the same speech (Schiff). The speaker filter can't separate these because the speaker is the same. Lowering k to 15, 20 or 25 cost recall or gained too little. Those near-duplicates rank high in BM25 because they share the true quote's words, so a smaller k doesn't remove them. Telling 'same statement, earlier wording' apart from 'source quote' is a verifier-prompt question. That knob is outside this line, and attempts to change it were marked invalid. I'm flagging it as the main lever for whoever controls the prompt.

That leaves retrieval. The 3 not_retrieved cases account for every recall@k miss (0.95 × 60 = 57). They are heavy paraphrases where the claim and the quote share almost no words ('hopeful' vs 'optimistic', 'grave matter' vs 'serious problem'). Two retrieval options haven't been tried on their own:
(a) the 'raw' query template, which costs no extra calls;
(b) the 'quotation' index (quote text only) with the current query, to see whether indexing speaker names lets the speaker's other quotes crowd out the true one. Every wrong match shown shares the speaker, which fits this idea.
Raising k to 40 alone (no surname filter) is the last option. It may recover a paraphrase case but adds a verifier batch: 2 calls per claim now suggests batches of 15, so k=40 would mean 3. It may also add same-speaker false matches, so it ranks last.

rationale: Every wrong earlier match shown comes from the same speaker as the true quote. With the quotation_speaker index, the speaker tokens in the query score every quote by that speaker, which pushes the speaker's other, similar quotes into the candidate set. With a quote-text-only index, ranking depends on wording, so wording that fits the claim more tightly should rank above loose same-speaker remarks like Schiff's or Netanyahu's. The cost per claim stays the same. Round 1 changed the template and the index together, so the index's effect on its own has never been measured.

'raw' is the only query template not yet tried. It keeps the speaker name and also the reporting verb ('said', 'argued', 'hopeful') and the full clause wording. That gives BM25 more terms to match on the heavy paraphrases that are currently missed, which are all of the recall@k misses. It costs no extra verifier calls. 'content', which drops the speaker, lost recall badly (0.75), so keeping the speaker tokens matters, and 'raw' keeps them.

The missed true quotes are paraphrases that probably rank just past 30. k=40 without the surname filter hasn't been tried; only k=40 combined with the filter was, and that combination may have dropped quotes with wrong attributions. The downsides are one more verifier batch per claim and possibly more same-speaker false matches, so this ranks below the options that cost nothing.
